lesson.title: When Proteins Team Up
lesson.summary: Quaternary structure describes how two or more independently folded polypeptide subunits come together, through the same noncovalent interactions that stabilize tertiary structure, to form one larger, functional protein complex.
lesson.body:
Not every protein stops at a single folded chain. When a functional protein is made of two or more separate polypeptide chains, each one already folded into its own tertiary structure, the way those chains fit together and interact is called quaternary structure. Each individual chain in this kind of arrangement is usually called a subunit, and a protein can have anywhere from two to many subunits, which may be identical to each other or completely different.

Hemoglobin is the classic example. It is built from four separate globin subunits, two identical alpha chains and two identical beta chains, each one folded into its own compact tertiary structure and each one holding its own heme group capable of binding a single oxygen molecule. The four subunits sit together in a specific quaternary arrangement, and that arrangement is not just structural, it is functional: when one subunit binds oxygen, it shifts shape slightly, and that shift is transmitted to the neighboring subunits, increasing their own affinity for oxygen. This behavior, called cooperative binding, lets hemoglobin pick up oxygen efficiently in the lungs and release it efficiently in oxygen poor tissues, and it is only possible because hemoglobin has quaternary structure at all.

The forces holding subunits together at the quaternary level are generally the same noncovalent interactions already described for tertiary structure: hydrophobic interactions between nonpolar patches on adjoining subunit surfaces, hydrogen bonds, and ionic bonds, occasionally reinforced by disulfide bonds between chains. Collagen offers a different pattern of multi chain assembly, three separate polypeptide chains wind around each other into a rope like triple helix stabilized in large part by hydrogen bonding, producing the tough, fibrous protein that gives connective tissue its strength.

It is important to be clear that quaternary structure is optional, not universal. Myoglobin, the oxygen storage protein discussed earlier, functions perfectly well as a single polypeptide chain and has no quaternary structure at all, while hemoglobin, built from essentially similar globin folds, only works properly because four of those folded chains are assembled together. Whether a protein stops at tertiary structure or goes on to quaternary structure depends entirely on what that protein needs to do.

Assembling multiple subunits into one complex offers real advantages beyond cooperative binding. It allows a cell to regulate protein activity by controlling whether subunits associate or separate, it can increase overall stability compared to a single large chain, and it allows different subunits with different jobs to be combined into one functional machine, as seen in multi subunit enzyme complexes such as DNA polymerase or ATP synthase.
